framework_name: Build vs Buy vs Fine-tune vs RAG Decision Matrix
creator_or_source: No single creator — this is a composite decision framework that emerged organically from the GenAI practitioner and enterprise consulting community (2023–2026). Key contributors include: Google Cloud ('To Tune or Not to Tune' guide, May 2024), AWS ('Tailoring Foundation Models' guide with open-source code on GitHub, 2024), IBM (RAG vs Fine-tuning vs Prompt Engineering comparison), IDC (GenAI Build vs Buy strategic framework, January 2024), a16z (Enterprise CIO survey on Build vs Buy with 100 Global 2000 executives, 2025), KPMG ('The Evolution of Build vs Buy', February 2025, and 'Agentic AI Untangled: Build, Buy, or Borrow', 2026), MarkTechPost (VP of AI Product weighted scoring decision framework, August 2025), Predibase (Build vs Buy ebook with TCO scoring rubric for GenAI infrastructure), Towards Data Science / Anurag Bhagat ('Build vs Buy Dilemma for GenAI Applications', January 2025), CIO.com ('Your next big AI decision isn't build vs buy — it's how to combine the two', December 2025), Microsoft (AI Decision Framework with BXT scorecard, January 2026), and Deloitte (Agentic AI Strategy report in Tech Trends 2026). The framework synthesizes the traditional software build-vs-buy methodology (McKinsey, Gartner heritage) with GenAI-specific technical dimensions (RAG, fine-tuning, prompt engineering, pre-training, and increasingly agentic AI) that arose from the LLM deployment wave starting in 2023.
year_introduced: 2023–2024 (the traditional build-vs-buy framework dates back decades in software engineering, but the four-option GenAI variant — Build / Buy API-SaaS / Fine-tune / RAG — crystallized in 2023–2024 as enterprises moved from LLM experimentation to production deployment. By 2025–2026, a fifth dimension — Agentic AI / compound AI systems — has entered the matrix, and the dominant framing has shifted from 'choose one' to 'assemble a blend')
scope: Decision-making — Covers the strategic and technical choice between four core AI implementation approaches (plus emerging agentic fifth option): (1) Build custom models from scratch (pre-training), (2) Buy API/SaaS solutions (OpenAI API, Anthropic, Google Vertex AI, Mistral AI, etc.), (3) Fine-tune existing foundation models on domain-specific data, (4) Implement RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) over off-the-shelf models, (5) Deploy agentic AI / compound AI systems (emerging, 2025–2026). Also addresses hybrid/blended/'assembled' approaches combining multiple options, which per CIO.com (December 2025) and KPMG AI Pulse Survey (2026) now represent the dominant enterprise pattern. Does not cover the full project lifecycle (deployment, monitoring, MLOps) — those require complementary frameworks.
key_components:
The Build vs Buy vs Fine-tune vs RAG Decision Matrix is structured around four core implementation approaches (plus an emerging fifth) evaluated against multiple decision dimensions:

**The Four Core Approaches (+ Emerging Fifth)**

1. **Build (Pre-train from scratch)**: Train a foundation model on proprietary data from the ground up. Requires massive compute (thousands of GPU-hours), large curated datasets, and specialized ML teams. Examples: Bloomberg training BloombergGPT on financial data, or a defense contractor building a sovereign model. Cost range: $1M–$100M+. Timeline: 6–18 months. Gives maximum control and IP ownership but is only justified when no existing model covers your domain or when data sovereignty demands it. Per McKinsey State of AI November 2025, only 7% of organizations have fully scaled AI — most that attempt Build never reach production.

2. **Buy (API/SaaS)**: Use commercial LLM APIs (OpenAI GPT-4o/GPT-5, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, Mistral AI) or AI-powered SaaS products (Jasper, Copy.ai, Glean, etc.) via subscription or pay-per-token pricing. Fastest path to production (days to weeks). Minimal engineering required. Cost (2025–2026 pricing): GPT-4o at $5/$20 per million tokens input/output, Claude Sonnet at $3/$15, Gemini 2.5 Pro at $1.25–$10, DeepSeek at $0.28/$0.42 per million — a 92% reduction in GPT-4 input costs since March 2023. SaaS products range $20–$500/seat/month. Per the a16z 2025 survey of 100 Global 2000 CIOs, off-the-shelf AI-native third-party applications are eclipsing custom builds, with over 90% of respondents testing third-party apps for customer support. Risks include vendor lock-in, limited customization, data privacy concerns (data sent to third-party servers), and ongoing token costs that scale linearly with usage. 81% of enterprise CIOs now use 3+ model families, up from 68% a year prior.

3. **Fine-tune**: Take a pre-trained foundation model (open-source like Llama 3, Mistral, or commercial via API) and further train it on your domain-specific dataset using techniques like LoRA, QLoRA, or full fine-tuning. Cost range: $100–$50K per training run depending on model size and method — QLoRA on a Llama-2 7B model can run on a single RTX 4090 (24GB VRAM) at $0.40–$0.80/hour on cloud, achieving 95–99% of full fine-tune performance; full fine-tuning of a 7B model requires ~120GB VRAM and ~$50K in H100 GPUs ($2.10–$4.00/hour). PEFT methods (LoRA, QLoRA) reduce costs 10–20x compared to full fine-tuning while retaining 90–95% quality. Timeline: days to weeks for training, plus data preparation. Produces a specialized model that 'knows' your domain vocabulary, formatting preferences, and reasoning patterns. Best when you need consistent output style, specialized terminology, or performance on narrow tasks that general models handle at only 60–70% accuracy. Per LangChain State of Agent Engineering 2025, 57% of organizations are NOT fine-tuning, relying instead on base models + prompt engineering + RAG.

4. **RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)**: Keep the base model unchanged but connect it to an external knowledge base (vector database, document store) from which relevant context is retrieved at query time and injected into the prompt. Implementation cost: $5K–$50K for initial setup (embedding pipeline, vector DB, retrieval logic). Ongoing cost: vector DB hosting ranges widely — Pinecone Standard from $50/month, Enterprise from $500/month, self-hosted Milvus on AWS $200–$500/month, full private RAG infrastructure $5K–$8K/month for enterprise workloads. Timeline: 1–4 weeks for MVP. Best when data changes frequently, when you need source citations, or when factual accuracy on proprietary data is critical. Over 55% of enterprises piloting GenAI in 2025 prioritize RAG implementations, citing up to 40% faster decision-making and 25% higher employee productivity. A developer built a production RAG system for as low as $5/month using budget-optimized architecture (Dev.to, 2025).

5. **Agentic AI / Compound AI Systems (emerging, 2025–2026)**: Orchestrate multiple AI models, tools, and retrieval systems into autonomous or semi-autonomous agent workflows. Rather than a single model call, agentic systems plan, execute multi-step tasks, use tools, and self-correct. Per KPMG AI Pulse Survey 2026, 57% of organizations favor a blended build-buy-borrow approach for AI agents (up from 51% in prior quarter). Per Deloitte Tech Trends 2026, agentic AI is the top enterprise AI trend. The decision is not 'build vs buy an agent' but how to assemble: buy foundation models, adopt vendor-provided domain agents, build custom orchestration and retrieval, and connect everything under shared governance rails. Per McKinsey State of AI November 2025, 23% of respondents report scaling agentic AI systems, with an additional 39% experimenting.

**Decision Dimensions (the evaluation criteria)**

- **Competitive advantage**: Does AI capability drive differentiation within 12–24 months? If yes, lean Build or Fine-tune. If commoditized, Buy. Per MarkTechPost framework: Build if Build score exceeds Buy by 20%+ on weighted criteria; Buy if vice versa; Blend if within +/-20%.
- **Data freshness**: How often does your knowledge base change? Daily/weekly → RAG. Annually or stable domain → Fine-tune. Static and proprietary → Build. Emerging alternative for agents: contextual/agentic memory that stores and retrieves information over extended periods.
- **Data privacy & sovereignty**: Can data leave your infrastructure? No → Build or Fine-tune with on-premise deployment, or RAG with self-hosted model. Yes → Buy API is acceptable. Key for EU context: Mistral AI (French, EU-hosted) offers sovereign infrastructure — Mistral Compute launching 2026 with 18,000 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell chips powered by nuclear energy, no exposure to US CLOUD Act. ASML invested EUR 1.5B in Mistral at EUR 12B valuation.
- **Budget and TCO**: Per the a16z 2025 CIO survey, LLM budgets are growing ~75% YoY. Break-even for custom AI vs API occurs at approximately $15K/month in API spend (18–24 month horizon). RAG TCO is 10–50x lower per experiment than fine-tuning pipelines. Fine-tuning via QLoRA becomes cost-effective at >5M tokens of monthly usage (reduced prompt length by 50%+). Critical cost trend: GPT-4 input pricing dropped 92% from $30/M tokens (March 2023) to $2.50/M tokens (GPT-4o cached, 2025) — cost thresholds shift quarterly.
- **Team capability**: Build requires senior ML engineers ($200K–$400K/year). Fine-tune requires ML engineers with training expertise (PEFT methods lower the bar significantly). RAG requires data engineers and retrieval expertise. Buy requires minimal technical staff (product managers, prompt engineers). Agentic systems require orchestration skills (LangChain, AutoGen, CrewAI familiarity).
- **Time to value**: Buy = days. RAG = 1–4 weeks. Fine-tune = 2–8 weeks. Agentic MVP = 2–6 weeks. Build = 6–18 months.
- **Quality requirements**: If general models achieve >90% accuracy → Buy or RAG. If 60–70% and you need >90% → Fine-tune (achieves 91% accuracy for classification tasks per arxiv:2503.24307). If no existing model covers your domain → Build.
- **Regulatory compliance**: EU AI Act (high-risk applications may require Build/Fine-tune for auditability — fines up to EUR 35M or 7% global annual revenue), GDPR (Schrems II transfer concerns — favors EU-hosted solutions), NIST AI RMF (governance maturity alignment). The German Data Protection Conference (DSK) published RAG-specific GDPR guidance v1.0 (October 2025) confirming RAG can have significant positive impact on privacy compliance (accuracy principle: reduced hallucination through grounding) while noting risks around data minimization, transparency, and external data flows.

**The Decision Flowchart (simplified)**

1. Start with prompt engineering on a commercial API (Buy) — if performance is satisfactory, stop here.
2. If the model lacks domain knowledge but data changes frequently → add RAG.
3. If the model lacks domain knowledge and data is stable → Fine-tune.
4. If you need the model to change its behavior, style, or output format consistently → Fine-tune.
5. If no existing foundation model covers your domain, or sovereignty requires it → Build.
6. If you need both current knowledge AND specialized behavior → Hybrid (Fine-tune + RAG).
7. If you need multi-step autonomous workflows with tool use → Agentic architecture (typically RAG + orchestration + bought models).

Important: Per The New Stack (2025), this is 'not a ladder' — do not treat it as a linear progression. Production systems are developed by being constrained, not by being sophisticated. Choose the simplest approach that meets requirements.

**The Hybrid/Assembled Approach (2025–2026 consensus)**

Per CIO.com (December 2025), the a16z enterprise survey, and KPMG Agentic AI report (2026), the dominant pattern is 'assembled' solutions: buy foundation models, adopt vendor-provided domain agents, build custom retrieval and orchestration, and connect everything under shared governance and orchestration rails — what CIOs call an 'opinionated enterprise AI platform.' KPMG (February 2025) confirms that the decision is no longer binary — organizations need a flexible approach. The 'last mile' (custom retrieval, tool adapters, evaluation datasets, hallucination tests, sector-specific guardrails) remains enterprise IP even when the base model is bought. Microsoft's AI Decision Framework (January 2026) formalizes this with a BXT (Business-Experience-Technology) scorecard: every AI initiative must prove Business viability, Experience desirability, and Technology feasibility before funding.

**Cost Threshold Benchmarks (2025–2026 data)**

- API costs <$5K/month: Buy (API/SaaS) is clearly optimal
- API costs $5K–$15K/month: Evaluate Fine-tune or RAG to reduce costs
- API costs >$15K/month: Strong case for Fine-tune or Build
- Advanced/enterprise AI systems: $150K–$500K+ (can exceed $1M for healthcare/finance)
- RAG infrastructure: $50–$8K/month depending on scale (from budget self-hosted to enterprise private)
- Fine-tuning run (QLoRA): $100–$5K per experiment; full fine-tuning: $5K–$50K per experiment
- Pre-training from scratch: $1M–$100M+
- Ongoing operational costs (any approach): $3K–$10K/month for maintenance
- Ultra-budget LLM option: DeepSeek at $0.70 per million tokens (blended I/O), 50x cheaper than GPT-4o
- Batch API discount: OpenAI offers 50% cost reduction for asynchronous batch processing
typical_use_case: A French e-commerce startup building an AI customer service assistant must decide how to implement it. They start by testing Claude API (Buy approach) with prompt engineering — it handles 70% of queries well but fails on product-specific questions and company policies. They then implement RAG by indexing their product catalog, FAQ database, and return policies into a vector store — this brings accuracy to 90% for factual questions. However, the assistant's tone is inconsistent and doesn't match their brand voice. They fine-tune a Mistral 7B model on 5,000 examples of their ideal customer service conversations using QLoRA (cost: ~EUR 500 for the training run on a cloud RTX 4090), then combine it with RAG for real-time product data. Total setup: 6 weeks, ~EUR 12K, 2 engineers. The decision matrix guided them through the progression from Buy → RAG → Fine-tune+RAG hybrid, avoiding the trap of over-engineering (Build) or under-investing (Buy-only). As the startup scales to handle 50K customer queries/month by Year 2, the self-hosted Mistral fine-tuned model saves approximately EUR 2K/month versus equivalent API costs, making the Fine-tune+RAG hybrid the most cost-effective choice at that volume.
deliverables: A scored decision (Build / Buy / Fine-tune / RAG / Hybrid-Assembled / Agentic) with justification across multiple weighted dimensions. Optionally: a filled scoring rubric per the MarkTechPost framework (1–5 per dimension, weighted by strategic priority, with a 20% threshold rule for Build vs Buy vs Blend), a 3-year TCO projection comparing approaches (factoring in the ~92% annual API price decline trend), a risk register covering vendor lock-in, data privacy, and regulatory compliance, a BXT (Business-Experience-Technology) viability check per Microsoft's AI Decision Framework, and a phased implementation roadmap (typically: start Buy/RAG, evolve to Fine-tune/Hybrid as usage scales, add agentic orchestration for complex workflows).
genai_relevance: High — This framework exists specifically because of Generative AI. The traditional build-vs-buy decision for classical ML was primarily binary (build your own model vs. buy a vendor solution). The GenAI era introduced two new middle options — Fine-tuning and RAG — that did not exist as mainstream choices before 2023. Fine-tuning foundation models via parameter-efficient methods (LoRA, QLoRA) became accessible in 2023, and RAG emerged as a standard architecture pattern in 2023–2024. By 2025–2026, agentic AI / compound AI systems are emerging as a fifth dimension. The framework directly addresses GenAI-specific concerns: foundation model selection, prompt engineering as a first resort, token economics (with prices dropping 92% in 2 years), hallucination mitigation (RAG's citation advantage, confirmed by DSK GDPR guidance as supporting the accuracy principle), context window management, the 'context bloat' cost problem with RAG at scale, multi-model portfolio strategies (81% of enterprise CIOs use 3+ model families per a16z 2025), and orchestration of assembled solutions. Over 55% of enterprises piloting GenAI in 2025 prioritize RAG implementations. The a16z 2025 survey found that off-the-shelf AI-native third-party applications are eclipsing custom builds for most use cases, confirming the Buy+RAG pattern as the dominant first choice. Per McKinsey November 2025, 88% of organizations use AI but only 7% have fully scaled — the Build vs Buy decision remains the primary bottleneck.
accessibility_for_non_engineers: High — The core decision ('should we build, buy, customize, or augment?') maps directly to business strategy concepts that MBA students understand. The framework uses familiar analogies: Build = developing proprietary software, Buy = subscribing to SaaS, Fine-tune = customizing an off-the-shelf product, RAG = giving an employee access to a company knowledge base, Agentic = hiring an autonomous assistant with tools. The scoring rubric dimensions (competitive advantage, cost, time-to-market, team capability) are standard business strategy criteria. Non-engineers can meaningfully participate in the decision by focusing on the business dimensions (competitive differentiation, budget, timeline, vendor risk) while collaborating with engineers on technical dimensions (data architecture, model performance, infrastructure). The decision flowchart is intuitive: 'start simple, escalate only when needed.' The MarkTechPost scoring approach (score 1–5 per dimension, weight by priority, apply 20% threshold) is accessible to any business student with spreadsheet skills.
time_to_apply: 1–2 hours for a structured team discussion using the decision dimensions. A full scoring exercise with TCO modeling takes a half-day workshop. Microsoft's BXT viability check adds 30–60 minutes upfront to validate business viability, experience desirability, and technology feasibility before diving into the Build vs Buy specifics. The actual implementation of the chosen approach ranges from days (Buy) to months (Build), but the decision itself is fast.
free_or_paid: Free — The framework is a synthesis of publicly available resources. Key free sources include: Google Cloud blog guide (May 2024), AWS blog guide with open-source code on GitHub (aws-samples/tailoring-foundation-models-for-business-needs-guide-to-rag-fine-tuning-hybrid-approaches), IBM comparison articles, a16z enterprise survey report, KPMG insights articles, Microsoft AI Decision Framework on GitHub (microsoft/Microsoft-AI-Decision-Framework, January 2026), and numerous blog posts and Medium articles. Predibase offers a gated but free ebook with TCO scoring rubric. IDC's full report requires registration. No paid tool is required to apply the framework — it can be conducted as a whiteboard exercise or spreadsheet scoring.
adoption_level: Widely adopted — While not a single branded framework with a canonical name, the build-vs-buy-vs-fine-tune-vs-RAG decision is now a standard strategic checkpoint in enterprise AI deployments. The a16z 2025 CIO survey (100 Global 2000 executives, 88% with >$1B revenue), McKinsey State of AI November 2025 (88% of organizations using AI), and IDC GenAI framework all treat this as a foundational decision. Major cloud providers (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure) all publish guides framing this exact decision. Microsoft formalized their version with the AI Decision Framework (January 2026). The specific term 'Build vs Buy vs Fine-tune vs RAG' appears across Towards Data Science, Medium, Dev.to, corporate blogs (Matillion, CoreWeave, Heavybit, InterSystems, Kanerika), consulting publications (KPMG, McKinsey, Deloitte), and academic research (arxiv:2503.24307 on systematic evaluation of LLM strategies). It is the de facto decision framework for any organization deploying LLM-based solutions. KPMG reports that 57% of organizations now favor blended approaches (2026), confirming the 'assembled' pattern as mainstream.
ai_project_stage: Multiple — Primarily serves the PoC and MVP stages (choosing the right technical approach before significant investment), but revisited at Scale stage (when API costs at >$15K/month justify migration to Fine-tune or Build) and at Maintenance stage (when data freshness requirements suggest adding RAG to a fine-tuned model, or when workflow complexity warrants agentic orchestration). Per McKinsey 2025, only one-third of companies have begun scaling AI — the framework is critical at the Ideation-to-PoC transition where most projects currently sit.
relevance_for_entrepreneurs: Critical for AI startup founders and intrapreneurs. Key benefits: (1) Prevents the most common startup mistake — over-engineering by building from scratch when an API+RAG solution would ship in weeks instead of months. The framework's 'start simple, escalate when needed' philosophy directly maps to lean startup methodology. (2) Enables informed cost projections: founders can model their unit economics across all four approaches — API token costs at projected query volumes (with prices dropping ~92% over 2 years, projections must account for deflation), fine-tuning investment amortized over users (QLoRA makes this accessible at ~$500 per training run for 7B models), RAG infrastructure costs, etc. The break-even at ~$15K/month API spend is a critical planning threshold. (3) De-risks investor conversations: showing that you've evaluated all options and chosen deliberately signals technical maturity. The MarkTechPost scoring rubric creates 'audit-ready evidence for boards and regulators.' (4) Helps navigate the European context: French/EU startups must factor in GDPR, EU AI Act compliance (fines up to EUR 35M or 7% global revenue), and data sovereignty — the framework's regulatory dimension directly addresses when to prefer self-hosted (Fine-tune with Mistral on OVHcloud/Scaleway) over API-based (Buy with US providers) approaches. Mistral AI's EUR 12B valuation and upcoming sovereign compute infrastructure make it the natural choice for EU-focused startups. (5) Supports pivot decisions: as the startup scales, the matrix helps decide when to migrate from Buy to Fine-tune, or from RAG to Agentic — these are common inflection points that can make or break unit economics. (6) Multi-model portfolio: per a16z 2025, 81% of enterprise CIOs use 3+ model families — startups should plan for model diversity from day one rather than betting on a single provider.
session_mapping: S3 (Projects) — directly supports the 'Framing & managing AI projects' theme, specifically the Build vs Buy decision. Also relevant to S4 (Business Models) for unit economics implications of each approach, and S1 (Fundamentals) for understanding the AI landscape and the role of different technical approaches.
complements: Pairs naturally with the AI Project Canvas (which scopes the project's 'what' and 'why' before this framework addresses the 'how'). Complements CRISP-DM/CRISP-ML(Q) (which provides the full project lifecycle methodology — the Build vs Buy decision typically occurs during the 'Data Understanding' and 'Modeling' phases of CRISP-DM). Also pairs with Andrew Ng's AI Transformation Playbook (Step 2: 'Build an in-house AI team' and Step 4: 'Develop an AI strategy' both require Build vs Buy decisions). For teams that choose Fine-tune or Build, MLOps frameworks and the ML Canvas become the next step. For teams evaluating costs, this framework connects to AI business model analysis (session 4 content on unit economics and scaling). The Value Proposition Canvas for AI helps validate whether the chosen approach actually delivers customer value. Microsoft's BXT (Business-Experience-Technology) scorecard complements as an upstream viability filter before applying the Build vs Buy matrix.
limitations: 1. **Rapidly evolving landscape**: Cost benchmarks and capability thresholds change quarterly as model prices drop (GPT-4 input pricing fell 92% from March 2023 to 2025; GPT-5 nano launched at $0.05/$0.40 per million tokens) and new approaches emerge (agentic AI, contextual memory, compound AI systems). Any cost-based decision made today may be invalidated within 6 months. 2. **No single canonical source**: Unlike CRISP-DM or the Business Model Canvas, there is no one authoritative document — practitioners must synthesize from multiple sources (Google, AWS, IBM, a16z, KPMG, etc.), which increases the risk of inconsistent application. 3. **Oversimplifies hybrid reality**: Most production deployments use blended approaches (e.g., bought API + RAG + fine-tuned embeddings + agentic orchestration), but the four-option framing can create a false sense that you must choose one. Per The New Stack (2025), treating the options as a linear ladder is a common mistake. 4. **Bias toward 'Buy first'**: The framework's 'start simple' philosophy may lead risk-averse teams to over-rely on vendor APIs, accumulating vendor lock-in and technical debt. Per KPMG, buying trades faster results for limited customization. 5. **Does not address evaluation methodology**: Choosing an approach is only half the battle — the framework does not specify how to measure whether your choice is working (evaluation metrics, A/B testing, human review protocols). 6. **Limited ethics/fairness coverage**: The regulatory dimension touches EU AI Act compliance but does not deeply address bias in fine-tuning data, hallucination risks across approaches, or the environmental impact of pre-training. 7. **Context bloat blind spot**: RAG's per-query cost scaling (injecting thousands of tokens per retrieval) is often underestimated in initial cost models, leading to budget surprises at scale — the framework should but does not always flag this prominently. 8. **Agentic dimension still immature**: While 23% of enterprises are scaling agentic AI per McKinsey 2025 and 57% favor blended agent approaches per KPMG 2026, the agentic option lacks mature decision criteria, cost models, and evaluation benchmarks compared to the four established options. 9. **ROI measurement gap**: Per McKinsey 2025, only 39% of organizations report any measurable EBIT impact from AI, and most estimate less than 5% — the framework helps choose an approach but does not guarantee the chosen approach delivers business value.
example_application:
A Paris-based legaltech startup wants to build an AI contract review assistant for French SMEs. Using the Build vs Buy vs Fine-tune vs RAG Decision Matrix:

**Step 1 — Competitive advantage assessment**: Contract review is the startup's core product, so AI quality is a direct competitive differentiator. This argues against a pure Buy approach (same API available to competitors). MarkTechPost scoring: Build scores higher on competitive advantage (4/5) vs Buy (2/5).

**Step 2 — Data freshness**: French legal texts (Code Civil, Code du Commerce) are updated annually. Client contracts use stable templates. Verdict: data is moderately stable → Fine-tune is a candidate.

**Step 3 — Data privacy**: Client contracts contain highly sensitive PII. GDPR requires data minimization. Sending full contracts to US-based API providers raises Schrems II transfer concerns. The DSK GDPR guidance on RAG (October 2025) notes that retrieval sources should be restricted to internal sources for privacy compliance. Verdict: must self-host or use EU-based providers → eliminates pure Buy with US APIs. Mistral AI (French, EU-hosted, EUR 12B valuation, upcoming sovereign compute with ASML backing) becomes the preferred base model.

**Step 4 — Budget**: Seed-stage startup, EUR 50K AI budget for Year 1.
- Buy (Mistral API): ~EUR 2K/month at projected volumes → EUR 24K/year, fast but no differentiation
- Fine-tune Mistral 7B via QLoRA: EUR 500 training run + EUR 1K/month hosting on Scaleway GPU → EUR 12.5K/year, specialized
- RAG on Mistral API: EUR 2K/month API + EUR 200/month self-hosted Milvus → EUR 26.4K/year, accurate but expensive at scale
- Hybrid (Fine-tune + RAG): EUR 500 training + EUR 1.2K/month hosting → EUR 14.9K/year, best quality

**Step 5 — Team capability**: 1 ML engineer + 1 full-stack developer. Can handle QLoRA fine-tuning and RAG (lower bar than full fine-tuning). Cannot pre-train from scratch.

**Step 6 — BXT viability check**: Business viability (strong: legal market EUR 5B+ in France), Experience desirability (high: SMEs need affordable contract review), Technology feasibility (confirmed: Mistral 7B + QLoRA + RAG is proven stack).

**Decision**: Hybrid approach — Fine-tune Mistral 7B via QLoRA on 10,000 annotated French contract clauses for legal reasoning and terminology, then add RAG for accessing the latest versions of French legal codes and client-specific contract templates. Deploy self-hosted in EU cloud (Scaleway or OVHcloud) for GDPR compliance. Plan migration to Mistral Compute when available in 2026.

**Timeline**: 4 weeks to MVP, EUR 14.9K projected Year 1 cost, full GDPR compliance, competitive differentiation through specialized legal reasoning that generic APIs cannot match. As the EU AI Act high-risk application deadlines approach (extended to December 2027 for some requirements), the self-hosted approach provides the auditability that regulators will require.
available_templates: No single canonical template exists, but several free resources provide structured decision aids: (1) Google Cloud blog guide with decision flowchart (cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/to-tune-or-not-to-tune, May 2024), (2) AWS open-source code and comparison guide on GitHub (github.com/aws-samples/tailoring-foundation-models-for-business-needs-guide-to-rag-fine-tuning-hybrid-approaches), (3) IBM comparison article with decision criteria table (ibm.com/think/topics/rag-vs-fine-tuning-vs-prompt-engineering), (4) InterSystems interactive decision tool with practical examples (intersystems.com/resources/rag-vs-fine-tuning-vs-prompt-engineering), (5) Predibase free ebook with TCO scoring rubric for build-vs-buy (go.predibase.com/en/build-vs-buy-ebook-lp), (6) MarkTechPost weighted scoring framework for VPs with 20% threshold rule (marktechpost.com, August 2025), (7) Microsoft AI Decision Framework with BXT scorecard on GitHub (microsoft/Microsoft-AI-Decision-Framework, January 2026), (8) Demand Metric build vs buy decision matrix template (demandmetric.com/content/build-vs-buy-decision-matrix). The framework can be applied as a spreadsheet scoring exercise using the decision dimensions listed above.
regulatory_alignment: EU AI Act (risk classification affects whether you can use third-party APIs for high-risk applications — may require Build/Fine-tune for auditability; fines up to EUR 35M or 7% global annual revenue; high-risk system requirements originally due August 2026 now expected to be extended to December 2027 per the EU Digital Omnibus), GDPR (data sent to US-based API providers raises transfer concerns under Schrems II — favors self-hosted Fine-tune or RAG with EU models like Mistral; the EU Digital Omnibus of November 2025 proposes clarifying how personal data including some special-category data can be used for AI development), German Data Protection Conference / DSK RAG guidance v1.0 (October 2025, confirming RAG supports accuracy principle while flagging data minimization and transparency risks, recommending measures including restricting retrieval to internal sources, anonymizing prompts, minimizing logging, and maintaining data rights management), NIST AI RMF (the governance maturity dimension of the framework aligns with NIST's risk management approach), ISO 42001 (AI management system standard — relevant for organizations choosing Build or Fine-tune where full lifecycle governance is needed).
